analysis.one_liner: Requires testing for lead in school and day care drinking water and funds pipe replacement.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in January 2019 with 60 cosponsors, it was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and stayed there until the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to set a lead action level for drinking water at schools and day care centers of no more than 15 parts per billion, required water systems that serve those facilities to sample for lead, and required water systems to notify schools, health agencies, and state and local officials within 24 hours when results hit that level. It also would have created federal grants to pay for testing and for replacing lead pipes and plumbing fixtures at schools. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children at schools and day care facilities, whose drinking water would be tested for lead and remediated where contamination is found. Parents, teachers, and school employees would get prompt notice and public access to test results, and school districts and state agencies would get grants to cover the cost of testing and replacing lead pipes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in schools and day cares

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to set a lead action level for school and day care drinking water at no more than 15 parts per billion within one year.

Requires public water systems to sample for lead at schools the EPA identifies as at risk, and to notify the school district, local health agencies, the municipality, and the state within 24 hours of results at or above the action level.

Creates a grant program for school districts and state agencies to test for lead and replace lead pipes, fittings, and fixtures with lead-free materials, with no more than 5 percent of funds going to administrative costs.
Requires grant recipients to post test results publicly online and notify parent, teacher, and employee organizations.

analysis.who_pays: Public water systems would bear the cost of sampling and 24-hour notification duties. Federal taxpayers would fund the grant program for testing and pipe replacement.

drawbacks.text: The bill's action level could be set as high as 15 parts per billion, a standard based on the existing federal lead rule rather than the lower trigger levels some health experts recommend for schools, where no amount of lead exposure is considered safe.
It would impose new sampling and rapid-notification duties on public water systems, and remediation grants would add federal spending, without a dedicated funding source in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — finding and fixing lead in the water children drink every day at school — is substantial and directly protects health. The 15 ppb ceiling is the bill's weakest point: it caps how strict the standard must be rather than guaranteeing the most protective one. The costs are real but conventional: utility sampling programs and federal grant spending, with 95 percent of grant money required to go to actual testing and remediation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brenda Lawrence introduced the Get the Lead Out of Schools Act on January 29, 2019.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day and no further action was taken.
Sixty House Democrats cosponsored the bill; the record lists no Republican cosponsors.

The bill would have required the EPA to set a lead action level of no more than 15 parts per billion for school and day care drinking water, mandated sampling and 24-hour notification by water systems, and created grants for testing and pipe replacement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public water systems avoided new federal sampling and 24-hour notification duties, and no federal money was spent on school testing or pipe replacement. Children in schools and day cares continue to drink water whose lead content is not systematically tested.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water utilities; school water stays untested

for.name: Brenda Lawrence
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require lead testing and remediation in school drinking water.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it without further action.

sides.party_line_note: All 60 cosponsors were House Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past the committee referral.

industries.note: The bill would have required utilities serving at-risk schools to sample for lead and notify school officials and health agencies within 24 hours of results, a new compliance cost. The public benefit — knowing when school water is contaminated — is exactly what the utilities would have had to pay to reveal.

Grant funds were earmarked for replacing lead pipes and fixtures with lead-free materials, creating paid work for testing labs and plumbing firms. That work coincides with the public's interest in removing lead.
